section_summary.extract_value: This section reviews the object–process dichotomy (Franzoi, 1995), arguing that women tend to view their bodies as objects (appearance-focused) whereas men tend to view bodies as processes (function-focused), and discusses evidence linking objectified views to negative outcomes for women. It notes limited direct research comparing body-as-process versus body-as-object, cites related findings (e.g., exercise and athletic involvement linked to more positive physical self-evaluations), and proposes that conversations about diet and exercise may differentially impact women's body image via the object–process distinction. The section does not label or describe any specific study as 'Study 1' or similar.
section_summary.evidence_source: When Franzoi (1995) introduced the object– process dichotomy in his analysis of gender  differences in body esteem, he argued that  women were more likely to focus their attention on how their bodies looked (body-asobject), whereas men were more likely to  focus their attention on how their bodies functioned (body-as-process), likely because of  gender roles.
